newsitem.title: USA: Clinton calls for racial unity.
newsitem.headline: Clinton calls for racial unity.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, in a fiery address on Saturday to prominent black leaders, appealed for racial unity and continued efforts to rid the United States of discrimination.

Speaking at the Congressional Black Caucus gala dinner, Clinton said he refused to abandon affirmative action programmes aimed at righting past discrimination because "there is still evidence that we have a way to go."

"If we're going to stay on the right track, we have to make sure that we have less discrimination, not more of it," Clinton told the 4,500 luminaries from politics, education, business and entertainment.
He said the United States was "blessed" by its diversity and this would be one of the strengths enabling the country to retain a leadership position in the world as it entered the new century.
"That's why I act so strongly when I see things like the church burnings or synagogues or Islamic centres being defaced. Any of this is wrong," he said.

Clinton cited the case of Bosnia, where a U.S.-sponsored ceasefire has ended four years of brutal fighting among Serbs, Croats and Moslems. Elections in Bosnia on Saturday were "a first halting step to moving toward the absence of war to the beginning of peace again," Clinton said.

Americans should learn about the tragic consequences of racial division and ethnic strife from the examples of Bosnia, Ireland, Burundi and Rwanda, and South Africa, Clinton said, noting that in each of those areas one group had defined itself by saying it was not the "other."
"We can never define ourselves as Americans by saying we are so good because we're not the other guy. The other guys are us too. We are all Americans," Clinton said.
The president also appealed to black leaders to help pull the nation's inner cities from the grip of economic stagnation with a new commitment to investment and jobs.
"If you are committed, I am committed," he said.
Clinton tried to find common ground with a core constituency that largely opposed his support of Republican-backed welfare reform legislation.

"I want you to remind America that you can't require people on welfare to go to work unless they have work," he said. "We cannot ever forget that there are still too many Americans who could no more come to this dinner than a man on the moon because they're still looking for a job and they need one tomorrow."

Despite angering many blacks by signing the welfare bill that critics say will cut millions of people from the rolls, polls suggest that African Americans still support the president and will do so in November's election.
